claims.subject: tretinoin (topical)
claims.text: In the EU, tretinoin is an authorised retinoid, including creams and gels for skin conditions such as acne (no centrally authorised tretinoin product was found; products are national); since EMA's 2018 review, topical retinoids must not be used in pregnancy or by women planning a pregnancy.
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "Retinoids include the active substances acitretin, adapalene, alitretinoin, bexarotene, isotretinoin, tazarotene and tretinoin. They are taken by mouth or applied as creams or gels to treat several conditions mainly affecting the skin, including severe acne and psoriasis. … Topical retinoids (those applied to the skin) must also not be used during pregnancy, and by women planning to have a baby." (English: "Retinoids include the active substances acitretin, adapalene, alitretinoin, bexarotene, isotretinoin, tazarotene and tretinoin. They are taken by mouth or applied as creams or gels to treat several conditions mainly affecting the skin, including severe acne and psoriasis. … Topical retinoids (those applied to the skin) must also not be used during pregnancy, and by women planning to have a baby.")

claims.subject: tretinoin (topical)
claims.text: In the EU, tretinoin (retinoic acid) is banned in cosmetics (Annex II entry 375), and the Commission's borderline manual says an anti-wrinkle product containing it that is marketed as a cosmetic is an illegal cosmetic (June 2025).
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "Some substances - such as tretinoin … are banned when used in cosmetic products. In this case, if anti -wrinkle products containing these ingredients are marketed as cosmetics, they are illegal cosmetics." (English: "Some substances - such as tretinoin … are banned when used in cosmetic products. In this case, if anti -wrinkle products containing these ingredients are marketed as cosmetics, they are illegal cosmetics.")

claims.subject: estradiol / menopausal hormone therapy
claims.text: In the EU, estradiol HRT is authorised nationally; the harmonised EU core product information (CMDh, December 2025) lists oestrogen-deficiency symptoms after menopause, osteoporosis prevention and vaginal atrophy as indications — skin is not an indication.
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "4.1 Therapeutic Indications … Hormone Replacement Therapy (HRT) for oestrogen deficiency symptoms in postmenopausal women. … Prevention of osteoporosis in postmenopausal women at high risk of future fractures who are intolerant of, or contraindicated for, other medicinal products approved for the prevention of osteoporosis. … Treatment of symptoms of vaginal atrophy due to oestrogen deficiency in postmenopausal women." (English: "4.1 Therapeutic Indications … Hormone Replacement Therapy (HRT) for oestrogen deficiency symptoms in postmenopausal women. … Prevention of osteoporosis in postmenopausal women at high risk of future fractures who are intolerant of, or contraindicated for, other medicinal products approved for the prevention of osteoporosis. … Treatment of symptoms of vaginal atrophy due to oestrogen deficiency in postmenopausal women.")

claims.subject: estradiol / menopausal hormone therapy
claims.text: The EU core product information for estradiol gels and sprays warns that estradiol can pass to children by skin contact, with reports of breast development, precocious puberty and gynaecomastia (CMDh, December 2025).
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "Estradiol spray/gel can be accidentally transferred to children from the area of the skin where it was sprayed/applied on. Post-marketing reports of breast budding and breast masses in prepubertal females, precocious puberty, gynaecomastia and breast masses in prepubertal males following unintentional secondary exposure to estradiol spray/gel have been reported." (English: "Estradiol spray/gel can be accidentally transferred to children from the area of the skin where it was sprayed/applied on. Post-marketing reports of breast budding and breast masses in prepubertal females, precocious puberty, gynaecomastia and breast masses in prepubertal males following unintentional secondary exposure to estradiol spray/gel have been reported.")

claims.subject: estradiol / menopausal hormone therapy
claims.text: In the EU, high-strength estradiol creams (100 micrograms/g, 0.01%) for vaginal atrophy are limited to a single treatment period of up to 4 weeks because estradiol is absorbed into the bloodstream (EMA PRAC, 16 January 2020; CMDh, 30 January 2020).
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "On 16 January 2020, EMA’s safety committee (PRAC) confirmed its recommendation to limit the use of high-strength creams containing 100 micrograms/gram (0.01%) of estradiol to a single treatment period of up to 4‑weeks. … The PRAC concluded that absorption of estradiol into the bloodstream is of concern and could result in similar side effects to those seen with hormone replacement therapy (HRT)." (English: "On 16 January 2020, EMA’s safety committee (PRAC) confirmed its recommendation to limit the use of high-strength creams containing 100 micrograms/gram (0.01%) of estradiol to a single treatment period of up to 4‑weeks. … The PRAC concluded that absorption of estradiol into the bloodstream is of concern and could result in similar side effects to those seen with hormone replacement therapy (HRT).")

claims.subject: estradiol / menopausal hormone therapy
claims.text: In the EU, oestrogens and progestogens are prohibited in cosmetic products (Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009, Annex II entries 260 and 194), so a hormone-containing 'cosmetic' skin cream is not lawful as a cosmetic.
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "cosmetic products shall not contain any of the following: … prohibited substances listed in Annex II … Progestogens … Oestrogens" (English: "cosmetic products shall not contain any of the following: … prohibited substances listed in Annex II … Progestogens … Oestrogens")

claims.subject: oral collagen
claims.text: In the EU, the Commission refused (Regulation (EU) No 1154/2014) a claim that a collagen peptide mixture maintains skin health by increasing elasticity and reducing wrinkles, because a cause-and-effect relationship was not established; the EU Register lists no authorised claim for collagen itself (searched 25 September 2026).
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "Characteristic collagen peptide mixture (collagen hydrolysate) having a beneficial physiological effect on the maintenance of skin health, as indicated by an increased skin elasticity and a reduction of wrinkles volume, by contributing to a normal collagen and elastin synthesis … a cause and effect relationship could not be established between the consumption of Verisol®P and the claimed effect. Accordingly, as the claim does not comply with the requirements of Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006, it should not be authorised." (English: "Characteristic collagen peptide mixture (collagen hydrolysate) having a beneficial physiological effect on the maintenance of skin health, as indicated by an increased skin elasticity and a reduction of wrinkles volume, by contributing to a normal collagen and elastin synthesis … a cause and effect relationship could not be established between the consumption of Verisol®P and the claimed effect. Accordingly, as the claim does not comply with the requirements of Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006, it should not be authorised.")

claims.subject: compounding
claims.text: In the EU, medicines prepared in a pharmacy for an individual patient on prescription (magistral formula) or to a pharmacopoeia for the pharmacy's own patients (officinal formula) are outside Directive 2001/83/EC, so they need no marketing authorisation under it (Article 3).
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "This Directive shall not apply to: … Any medicinal product prepared in a pharmacy in accordance with a medical prescription for an individual patient (commonly known as the magistral formula). … Any medicinal product which is prepared in a pharmacy in accordance with the prescriptions of a pharmacopoeia and is intended to be supplied directly to the patients served by the pharmacy in question (commonly known as the officinal formula)." (English: "This Directive shall not apply to: … Any medicinal product prepared in a pharmacy in accordance with a medical prescription for an individual patient (commonly known as the magistral formula). … Any medicinal product which is prepared in a pharmacy in accordance with the prescriptions of a pharmacopoeia and is intended to be supplied directly to the patients served by the pharmacy in question (commonly known as the officinal formula).")

claims.subject: compounding
claims.text: EU law exempts pharmacists who prepare medicines solely for retail supply in dispensing pharmacies from the manufacturing authorisation that all other manufacture needs (Directive 2001/83/EC, Article 40(2)).
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "However, such authorization shall not be required for preparation, dividing up, changes in packaging or presentation where these processes are carried out, solely for retail supply, by pharmacists in dispensing pharmacies or by persons legally authorized in the Member States to carry out such processes." (English: "However, such authorization shall not be required for preparation, dividing up, changes in packaging or presentation where these processes are carried out, solely for retail supply, by pharmacists in dispensing pharmacies or by persons legally authorized in the Member States to carry out such processes.")

claims.subject: unlicensed
claims.text: In the EU, no medicine may be placed on a member state's market without a national marketing authorisation or an EU-wide (central) authorisation (Directive 2001/83/EC, Article 6(1)).
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "No medicinal product may be placed on the market of a Member State unless a marketing authorisation has been issued by the competent authorities of that Member State in accordance with this Directive or an authorisation has been granted in accordance with Regulation (EC) No 726/2004" (English: "No medicinal product may be placed on the market of a Member State unless a marketing authorisation has been issued by the competent authorities of that Member State in accordance with this Directive or an authorisation has been granted in accordance with Regulation (EC) No 726/2004")

claims.subject: unlicensed
claims.text: EU law lets each member state, under its own legislation, allow an unauthorised medicine for an individual patient on a bona fide unsolicited order from an authorised health professional, under that professional's direct personal responsibility (Directive 2001/83/EC, Article 5(1)).
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "A Member State may, in accordance with legislation in force and to fulfil special needs, exclude from the provisions of this Directive medicinal products supplied in response to a bona fide unsolicited order, formulated in accordance with the specifications of an authorised health-care professional and for use by an individual patient under his direct personal responsibility." (English: "A Member State may, in accordance with legislation in force and to fulfil special needs, exclude from the provisions of this Directive medicinal products supplied in response to a bona fide unsolicited order, formulated in accordance with the specifications of an authorised health-care professional and for use by an individual patient under his direct personal responsibility.")

claims.subject: unlicensed
claims.text: EMA and HMA's shortage steering group asked EU prescribers in June 2024 to prescribe GLP-1 receptor agonists only for their authorised uses and said these medicines are not approved for, and should not be used for, cosmetic weight loss.
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "The MSSG therefore recommends that healthcare professionals prescribe these medicines in line with their authorised use(s) only, taking into account guidance issued by national authorities or applicable national therapeutic guidelines. GLP-1 receptor agonists are not approved for, and should not be used for, cosmetic weight loss, i.e. use for weight loss in people without obesity or people with overweight who do not have weight-related health problems." (English: "The MSSG therefore recommends that healthcare professionals prescribe these medicines in line with their authorised use(s) only, taking into account guidance issued by national authorities or applicable national therapeutic guidelines. GLP-1 receptor agonists are not approved for, and should not be used for, cosmetic weight loss, i.e. use for weight loss in people without obesity or people with overweight who do not have weight-related health problems.")

claims.subject: research-use-only
claims.text: Under EU law a product is a medicine by presentation (presented as treating or preventing disease) or by function (restoring, correcting or modifying physiological functions by a pharmacological, immunological or metabolic action), and where a product could be both a medicine and another regulated product, medicines law applies (Directive 2001/83/EC, Articles 1(2) and 2(2)).
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "Any substance or combination of substances presented as having properties for treating or preventing disease in human beings; or … Any substance or combination of substances which may be used in or administered to human beings either with a view to restoring, correcting or modifying physiological functions by exerting a pharmacological, immunological or metabolic action, or to making a medical diagnosis. … In cases of doubt, where, taking into account all its characteristics, a product may fall within the definition of a ‘medicinal product’ and within the definition of a product covered by other Community legislation the provisions of this Directive shall apply." (English: "Any substance or combination of substances presented as having properties for treating or preventing disease in human beings; or … Any substance or combination of substances which may be used in or administered to human beings either with a view to restoring, correcting or modifying physiological functions by exerting a pharmacological, immunological or metabolic action, or to making a medical diagnosis. … In cases of doubt, where, taking into account all its characteristics, a product may fall within the definition of a ‘medicinal product’ and within the definition of a product covered by other Community legislation the provisions of this Directive shall apply.")

claims.subject: research-use-only
claims.text: The research exclusion in Directive 2001/83/EC concerns medicinal products intended for research and development trials and is without prejudice to EU clinical-trials law (Article 3(3)).
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "Medicinal products intended for research and development trials, but without prejudice to the provisions of Directive 2001/20/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 4 April 2001 on the approximation of the laws, regulations and administrative provisions of the Member States relating to the implementation of good clinical practice in the conduct of clinical trials on medicinal products for human use" (English: "Medicinal products intended for research and development trials, but without prejudice to the provisions of Directive 2001/20/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 4 April 2001 on the approximation of the laws, regulations and administrative provisions of the Member States relating to the implementation of good clinical practice in the conduct of clinical trials on medicinal products for human use")

claims.subject: import
claims.text: Under EU law (Article 85c of Directive 2001/83/EC, inserted by the Falsified Medicines Directive 2011/62/EU), an online seller of medicines must be authorised in its member state, the medicines must comply with the law of the destination country, and the EU common logo must appear on every relevant page; member states may still ban online sale of prescription medicines.
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "Without prejudice to national legislation prohibiting the offer for sale at a distance of prescription medicinal products to the public by means of information society services … the natural or legal person offering the medicinal products is authorised or entitled to supply medicinal products to the public, also at a distance, in accordance with national legislation of the Member State in which that person is established … the medicinal products comply with the national legislation of the Member State of destination in accordance with Article 6(1) … the common logo referred to in paragraph 3 clearly displayed on every page of the website that relates to the offer for sale at a distance to the public of medicinal products" (English: "Without prejudice to national legislation prohibiting the offer for sale at a distance of prescription medicinal products to the public by means of information society services … the natural or legal person offering the medicinal products is authorised or entitled to supply medicinal products to the public, also at a distance, in accordance with national legislation of the Member State in which that person is established … the medicinal products comply with the national legislation of the Member State of destination in accordance with Article 6(1) … the common logo referred to in paragraph 3 clearly displayed on every page of the website that relates to the offer for sale at a distance to the public of medicinal products")

claims.subject: import
claims.text: Since 1 July 2015 every legally operating online pharmacy or retailer in the EU should display the common logo (Implementing Regulation (EU) No 699/2014), which links to the national register; a logo showing the EU flag is not legal (European Commission).
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "On 24 June 2014 the European Commission adopted the new common logo through Implementing Regulation 699/2014 . As of 1st of July 2015, all online pharmacies or retailers legally operating in the EU should display the logo. … Therefore, a logo displaying the EU flag, for example, would not be legal." (English: "On 24 June 2014 the European Commission adopted the new common logo through Implementing Regulation 699/2014 . As of 1st of July 2015, all online pharmacies or retailers legally operating in the EU should display the logo. … Therefore, a logo displaying the EU flag, for example, would not be legal.")

claims.subject: import
claims.text: EMA advises the public to buy medicines online only from retailers registered with national authorities, and to click the common logo and confirm the retailer is on the national register before buying.
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "Patients should only buy medicines from online retailers registered with the national competent authorities in the EU Member States, to reduce the risk of buying sub-standard or falsified medicines. … Click on the logo and confirm that the online pharmacy is listed on the national authority website" (English: "Patients should only buy medicines from online retailers registered with the national competent authorities in the EU Member States, to reduce the risk of buying sub-standard or falsified medicines. … Click on the logo and confirm that the online pharmacy is listed on the national authority website")

claims.subject: enforcement
claims.text: On 3 September 2025 EMA and HMA warned of a sharp rise in illegal medicines sold online and on social media as GLP-1 receptor agonists (semaglutide, liraglutide, tirzepatide); these products are unauthorised and may not contain the stated substance.
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "In recent months there has been a sharp rise in the number of illegal medicines marketed as GLP-1 receptor agonists such as semaglutide, liraglutide and tirzepatide for weight loss and diabetes. These products, often sold via fraudulent websites and promoted on social media, are not authorised and do not meet necessary standards of quality, safety and efficacy. … They may not contain the claimed active substance at all and may contain harmful levels of other substances." (English: "In recent months there has been a sharp rise in the number of illegal medicines marketed as GLP-1 receptor agonists such as semaglutide, liraglutide and tirzepatide for weight loss and diabetes. These products, often sold via fraudulent websites and promoted on social media, are not authorised and do not meet necessary standards of quality, safety and efficacy. … They may not contain the claimed active substance at all and may contain harmful levels of other substances.")

claims.subject: enforcement
claims.text: On 18 October 2023 EMA alerted EU patients and professionals that falsified pens labelled as Ozempic had been found at wholesalers in the EU (from Austria and Germany) and the UK, detected because their serial numbers scanned as inactive.
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "pre-filled pens falsely labelled as the diabetes medicine Ozempic (semaglutide, 1 mg, solution for injection) have been identified at wholesalers in the EU and the UK. … The pens, with labels in German, originated from wholesalers in Austria and Germany. … When the packs of the falsified Ozempic were scanned, the serial numbers were shown to be inactive, thereby alerting operators to a potential falsification." (English: "pre-filled pens falsely labelled as the diabetes medicine Ozempic (semaglutide, 1 mg, solution for injection) have been identified at wholesalers in the EU and the UK. … The pens, with labels in German, originated from wholesalers in Austria and Germany. … When the packs of the falsified Ozempic were scanned, the serial numbers were shown to be inactive, thereby alerting operators to a potential falsification.")

claims.subject: enforcement
claims.text: Europol's Operation SHIELD VI (April–November 2025, reported 25 February 2026) flagged counterfeit semaglutide products sold as fat-burners and dismantled a Spanish network supplying illegal medicines for cosmetic medicine to clinics, whose activities extended to Portugal.
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "Operation SHIELD VI highlighted several critical public health threats, including the proliferation of counterfeit Semaglutide-based products used as fat-burners … In Spain, the Guardia Civil and the Spanish Customs collaborated to dismantle a criminal organisation involved in the import, storage, and distribution of illegal medicines and health products for cosmetic medicine. … The criminal network’s activities extended to Portugal" (English: "Operation SHIELD VI highlighted several critical public health threats, including the proliferation of counterfeit Semaglutide-based products used as fat-burners … In Spain, the Guardia Civil and the Spanish Customs collaborated to dismantle a criminal organisation involved in the import, storage, and distribution of illegal medicines and health products for cosmetic medicine. … The criminal network’s activities extended to Portugal")

claims.subject: cosmetics
claims.text: In the EU, a cosmetic is a substance or mixture placed on the external parts of the body (skin, hair, nails, lips, external genitals) or teeth and oral mucosa, mainly to clean, perfume, change appearance, protect, keep in good condition or correct body odour (Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009, Article 2(1)(a)).
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "‘cosmetic product’ means any substance or mixture intended to be placed in contact with the external parts of the human body (epidermis, hair system, nails, lips and external genital organs) or with the teeth and the mucous membranes of the oral cavity with a view exclusively or mainly to cleaning them, perfuming them, changing their appearance, protecting them, keeping them in good condition or correcting body odours" (English: "‘cosmetic product’ means any substance or mixture intended to be placed in contact with the external parts of the human body (epidermis, hair system, nails, lips and external genital organs) or with the teeth and the mucous membranes of the oral cavity with a view exclusively or mainly to cleaning them, perfuming them, changing their appearance, protecting them, keeping them in good condition or correcting body odours")

claims.subject: cosmetics
claims.text: In the EU, anything intended to be ingested, inhaled, injected or implanted is not a cosmetic (Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009, Article 2(2)), so an injected peptide can never be a cosmetic.
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "a substance or mixture intended to be ingested, inhaled, injected or implanted into the human body shall not be considered to be a cosmetic product" (English: "a substance or mixture intended to be ingested, inhaled, injected or implanted into the human body shall not be considered to be a cosmetic product")

claims.subject: cosmetics
claims.text: The EU borderline manual (version 5.4, November 2024, retained in 5.5) says a product in a vial or ampoule for injection cannot be a cosmetic, and one sold as a cosmetic must be clearly for external use and not marketed with a device allowing injection or delivery below the epidermis.
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "If a substance or mixture presented in a vial or ampoule is for use by injection, then the product cannot be considered to meet the definition of a cosmetic product by virtue of Article 2(2) of the Cosmetics Regulation … Furthermore, the product should not be marketed with a device which could allow the injection of this product or its delivery below the epidermis" (English: "If a substance or mixture presented in a vial or ampoule is for use by injection, then the product cannot be considered to meet the definition of a cosmetic product by virtue of Article 2(2) of the Cosmetics Regulation … Furthermore, the product should not be marketed with a device which could allow the injection of this product or its delivery below the epidermis")

claims.subject: cosmetics
claims.text: The EU borderline manual says products used with needle rollers are cosmetics only if the product stays in the epidermis; if the needles reach the dermis, the product cannot be a cosmetic.
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "If the use of the roller only ena bles the application of the product in the epidermis, then the product is a cosmetic and its safety should be assessed taking into account the composition and the mode of delivery. On the other hand, if the needles reach the dermis, the use of the roller induces a deeper application of the product, and therefore this product cannot be qualified as a cosmetic." (English: "If the use of the roller only ena bles the application of the product in the epidermis, then the product is a cosmetic and its safety should be assessed taking into account the composition and the mode of delivery. On the other hand, if the needles reach the dermis, the use of the roller induces a deeper application of the product, and therefore this product cannot be qualified as a cosmetic.")

claims.subject: cosmetics
claims.text: Whether an EU product is a cosmetic is decided case by case by national authorities; the borderline manual says an anti-wrinkle product that significantly restores, corrects or modifies physiological functions by a pharmacological, immunological or metabolic action does not qualify as a cosmetic (June 2025).
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "However, some products presented as anti -wrinkle may significantly restore, correct or modify physiological functions by exerting a pharmacological, immunological or metabolic action. In that case, they would not qualify as cosmetics. … A decision on the qualification of the products has to be made by the na tional competent authorities on a case -by-case basis" (English: "However, some products presented as anti -wrinkle may significantly restore, correct or modify physiological functions by exerting a pharmacological, immunological or metabolic action. In that case, they would not qualify as cosmetics. … A decision on the qualification of the products has to be made by the na tional competent authorities on a case -by-case basis")

claims.subject: cosmetics
claims.text: The EU borderline manual notes that a product can act pharmacologically, and so fall outside cosmetics law, even when its ingredient is not used in any medicine, naming 'some specially designed peptides' in eyelash-growth products.
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "other substances with an influence on eyelash growth may exist (or be designed), which are not used as active drug ingredients, but the product containing them could still restore, correct or modify physiological functions by exerting a pharmacological, immunological or metabolic action (e.g. some specially designed peptides)." (English: "other substances with an influence on eyelash growth may exist (or be designed), which are not used as active drug ingredients, but the product containing them could still restore, correct or modify physiological functions by exerting a pharmacological, immunological or metabolic action (e.g. some specially designed peptides).")

claims.subject: cosmetics
claims.text: The EU borderline manual states that topical products working through hormones or hormone-like substances (its example: breast-augmentation products) act pharmacologically and cannot be cosmetics.
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "Topical breast augmentation products achieve their objective through the action of hormones … They therefore significantly " restore, correct or modify physiological functions by exerting a pharmacological, immunological or metabolic action " … and cannot be qualified as cosmetic products." (English: "Topical breast augmentation products achieve their objective through the action of hormones … They therefore significantly " restore, correct or modify physiological functions by exerting a pharmacological, immunological or metabolic action " … and cannot be qualified as cosmetic products.")

claims.subject: cosmetics
claims.text: EU cosmetics law also prohibits substances with androgenic effect and steroidal anti-androgens in cosmetic products (Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009, Annex II entries 37 and 390).
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "cosmetic products shall not contain any of the following: … prohibited substances listed in Annex II … Substances with androgenic effect … Anti-androgens of steroidal structure" (English: "cosmetic products shall not contain any of the following: … prohibited substances listed in Annex II … Substances with androgenic effect … Anti-androgens of steroidal structure")

claims.subject: cosmetics
claims.text: Before an EU cosmetic is placed on the market it needs a responsible person in the EU, a safety assessment with a cosmetic product safety report, and electronic notification to the Commission (Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009, Articles 4, 10 and 13).
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "Only cosmetic products for which a legal or natural person is designated within the Community as ‘responsible person’ shall be placed on the market. … the responsible person shall, prior to placing a cosmetic product on the market, ensure that the cosmetic product has undergone a safety assessment on the basis of the relevant information and that a cosmetic product safety report is set up in accordance with Annex I. … Prior to placing the cosmetic product on the market the responsible person shall submit, by electronic means, the following information to the Commission" (English: "Only cosmetic products for which a legal or natural person is designated within the Community as ‘responsible person’ shall be placed on the market. … the responsible person shall, prior to placing a cosmetic product on the market, ensure that the cosmetic product has undergone a safety assessment on the basis of the relevant information and that a cosmetic product safety report is set up in accordance with Annex I. … Prior to placing the cosmetic product on the market the responsible person shall submit, by electronic means, the following information to the Commission")

claims.subject: cosmetics
claims.text: In the EU, cosmetic labelling, marketing and advertising must not use text, names, pictures or signs implying that a product has characteristics or functions it does not have (Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009, Article 20(1)).
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "In the labelling, making available on the market and advertising of cosmetic products, text, names, trade marks, pictures and figurative or other signs shall not be used to imply that these products have characteristics or functions which they do not have." (English: "In the labelling, making available on the market and advertising of cosmetic products, text, names, trade marks, pictures and figurative or other signs shall not be used to imply that these products have characteristics or functions which they do not have.")

claims.subject: cosmetics
claims.text: EU cosmetic claims must be supported by adequate and verifiable evidence, and a claim that extrapolates an ingredient's properties (for example a peptide's) to the finished product needs evidence such as the ingredient's presence at an effective concentration (Regulation (EU) No 655/2013).
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "Claims for cosmetic products, whether explicit or implicit, shall be supported by adequate and verifiable evidence regardless of the types of evidential support used to substantiate them, including where appropriate expert assessments. … A claim extrapolating (explicitly or implicitly) ingredient properties to the finished product shall be supported by adequate and verifiable evidence, such as by demonstrating the presence of the ingredient at an effective concentration." (English: "Claims for cosmetic products, whether explicit or implicit, shall be supported by adequate and verifiable evidence regardless of the types of evidential support used to substantiate them, including where appropriate expert assessments. … A claim extrapolating (explicitly or implicitly) ingredient properties to the finished product shall be supported by adequate and verifiable evidence, such as by demonstrating the presence of the ingredient at an effective concentration.")

claims.subject: cosmetics
claims.text: The Commission's CosIng database is not legally binding: a listing does not determine an ingredient's regulatory status, which only Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 and its Annexes set (read 25 September 2026).
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "CosIng is a non-legally binding information database. It provides information on cosmetic ingredients but does not, in itself, determine their regulatory status. Only Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 and its Annexes establish whether, and under which conditions, substances may be used in cosmetic products." (English: "CosIng is a non-legally binding information database. It provides information on cosmetic ingredients but does not, in itself, determine their regulatory status. Only Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 and its Annexes establish whether, and under which conditions, substances may be used in cosmetic products.")

claims.subject: cosmetics
claims.text: Injectable dermal fillers without a medical purpose are regulated in the EU under the Medical Devices Regulation (EU) 2017/745 as Annex XVI products.
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "LIST OF GROUPS OF PRODUCTS WITHOUT AN INTENDED MEDICAL PURPOSE REFERRED TO IN ARTICLE 1(2) … Substances, combinations of substances, or items intended to be used for facial or other dermal or mucous membrane filling by subcutaneous, submucous or intradermal injection or other introduction, excluding those for tattooing." (English: "LIST OF GROUPS OF PRODUCTS WITHOUT AN INTENDED MEDICAL PURPOSE REFERRED TO IN ARTICLE 1(2) … Substances, combinations of substances, or items intended to be used for facial or other dermal or mucous membrane filling by subcutaneous, submucous or intradermal injection or other introduction, excluding those for tattooing.")

claims.subject: supplements
claims.text: In the EU, food supplements are foods that supplement the normal diet, are concentrated sources of nutrients or other substances with a nutritional or physiological effect, and are sold in measured doses such as capsules, tablets or sachets (Directive 2002/46/EC, Article 2(a)).
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "‘food supplements’ means foodstuffs the purpose of which is to supplement the normal diet and which are concentrated sources of nutrients or other substances with a nutritional or physiological effect, alone or in combination, marketed in dose form, namely forms such as capsules, pastilles, tablets, pills and other similar forms, sachets of powder, ampoules of liquids, drop dispensing bottles, and other similar forms of liquids and powders designed to be taken in measured small unit quantities" (English: "‘food supplements’ means foodstuffs the purpose of which is to supplement the normal diet and which are concentrated sources of nutrients or other substances with a nutritional or physiological effect, alone or in combination, marketed in dose form, namely forms such as capsules, pastilles, tablets, pills and other similar forms, sachets of powder, ampoules of liquids, drop dispensing bottles, and other similar forms of liquids and powders designed to be taken in measured small unit quantities")

claims.subject: supplements
claims.text: In the EU, a health claim on a food is prohibited unless it is authorised and included in the EU lists of authorised claims (Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006, Article 10(1)).
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "Health claims shall be prohibited unless they comply with the general requirements in Chapter II and the specific requirements in this Chapter and are authorised in accordance with this Regulation and included in the lists of authorised claims provided for in Articles 13 and 14." (English: "Health claims shall be prohibited unless they comply with the general requirements in Chapter II and the specific requirements in this Chapter and are authorised in accordance with this Regulation and included in the lists of authorised claims provided for in Articles 13 and 14.")

claims.subject: supplements
claims.text: The EU authorised claim linking collagen to skin is a vitamin C claim — 'Vitamin C contributes to normal collagen formation for the normal function of skin' — usable only on foods that are at least a source of vitamin C (Regulation (EU) No 432/2012).
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "Vitamin C contributes to normal collagen formation for the normal function of skin … The claim may be used only for food which is at least a source of vitamin C as referred to in the claim SOURCE OF [NAME OF VITAMIN/S] AND/OR [NAME OF MINERAL/S] as listed in the Annex to Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006." (English: "Vitamin C contributes to normal collagen formation for the normal function of skin … The claim may be used only for food which is at least a source of vitamin C as referred to in the claim SOURCE OF [NAME OF VITAMIN/S] AND/OR [NAME OF MINERAL/S] as listed in the Annex to Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006.")

claims.subject: supplements
claims.text: In the EU, food information, including advertising, must not attribute to any food the property of preventing, treating or curing a human disease (Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011, Article 7(3) and (4)).
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "food information shall not attribute to any food the property of preventing, treating or curing a human disease, nor refer to such properties. … Paragraphs 1, 2 and 3 shall also apply to: … advertising" (English: "food information shall not attribute to any food the property of preventing, treating or curing a human disease, nor refer to such properties. … Paragraphs 1, 2 and 3 shall also apply to: … advertising")

claims.subject: supplements
claims.text: In the EU, a food not consumed to a significant degree in the Union before 15 May 1997 (for example, one with a new molecular structure) is a novel food and may be sold only once authorised and listed in the Union list (Regulation (EU) 2015/2283, Articles 3 and 6).
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "‘novel food’ means any food that was not used for human consumption to a significant degree within the Union before 15 May 1997 … food with a new or intentionally modified molecular structure, where that structure was not used as, or in, a food within the Union before 15 May 1997 … Only novel foods authorised and included in the Union list may be placed on the market within the Union as such, or used in or on foods" (English: "‘novel food’ means any food that was not used for human consumption to a significant degree within the Union before 15 May 1997 … food with a new or intentionally modified molecular structure, where that structure was not used as, or in, a food within the Union before 15 May 1997 … Only novel foods authorised and included in the Union list may be placed on the market within the Union as such, or used in or on foods")

claims.subject: advertising
claims.text: EU law requires member states to prohibit any advertising of a medicine that has no marketing authorisation, and advertising of authorised medicines must match the summary of product characteristics (Directive 2001/83/EC, Article 87).
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "Member States shall prohibit any advertising of a medicinal product in respect of which a marketing authorization has not been granted in accordance with Community law. … All parts of the advertising of a medicinal product must comply with the particulars listed in the summary of product characteristics." (English: "Member States shall prohibit any advertising of a medicinal product in respect of which a marketing authorization has not been granted in accordance with Community law. … All parts of the advertising of a medicinal product must comply with the particulars listed in the summary of product characteristics.")

claims.subject: advertising
claims.text: EU law requires member states to prohibit advertising of prescription-only medicines to the general public (Directive 2001/83/EC, Article 88(1)(a)); 'advertising' includes any inducement designed to promote prescription, supply, sale or consumption (Article 86(1)).
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "‘advertising of medicinal products’ shall include any form of door-to-door information, canvassing activity or inducement designed to promote the prescription, supply, sale or consumption of medicinal products … Member States shall prohibit the advertising to the general public of medicinal products which: … are available on medical prescription only, in accordance with Title VI" (English: "‘advertising of medicinal products’ shall include any form of door-to-door information, canvassing activity or inducement designed to promote the prescription, supply, sale or consumption of medicinal products … Member States shall prohibit the advertising to the general public of medicinal products which: … are available on medical prescription only, in accordance with Title VI")

claims.subject: advertising
claims.text: Where EU law allows advertising of a medicine to the public, it must not refer to a recommendation by scientists, health professionals or celebrities, or suggest the medicine is a cosmetic (Directive 2001/83/EC, Article 90).
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "The advertising of a medicinal product to the general public shall not contain any material which: … refers to a recommendation by scientists, health professionals or persons who are neither of the foregoing but who, because of their celebrity, could encourage the consumption of medicinal products … suggests that the medicinal product is a foodstuff, cosmetic or other consumer product" (English: "The advertising of a medicinal product to the general public shall not contain any material which: … refers to a recommendation by scientists, health professionals or persons who are neither of the foregoing but who, because of their celebrity, could encourage the consumption of medicinal products … suggests that the medicinal product is a foodstuff, cosmetic or other consumer product")

claims.subject: advertising
claims.text: When medicines are promoted to prescribers or suppliers in the EU, no gifts, pecuniary advantages or benefits in kind may be offered unless inexpensive and relevant to practice, and prescribers must not solicit or accept prohibited inducements (Directive 2001/83/EC, Article 94).
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "Where medicinal products are being promoted to persons qualified to prescribe or supply them, no gifts, pecuniary advantages or benefits in kind may be supplied, offered or promised to such persons unless they are inexpensive and relevant to the practice of medicine or pharmacy. … Persons qualified to prescribe or supply medicinal products shall not solicit or accept any inducement prohibited under paragraph 1 or contrary to paragraph 2." (English: "Where medicinal products are being promoted to persons qualified to prescribe or supply them, no gifts, pecuniary advantages or benefits in kind may be supplied, offered or promised to such persons unless they are inexpensive and relevant to the practice of medicine or pharmacy. … Persons qualified to prescribe or supply medicinal products shall not solicit or accept any inducement prohibited under paragraph 1 or contrary to paragraph 2.")

claims.subject: advertising
claims.text: EU audiovisual law bans audiovisual commercial communications for prescription-only medicines and medical treatment, and video-sharing platforms must take measures to apply this to advertising on their services, including advertising they do not sell themselves (Directive 2010/13/EU, Articles 9(1)(f) and 28b(2)).
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "audiovisual commercial communications for medicinal products and medical treatment available only on prescription in the Member State within whose jurisdiction the media service provider falls shall be prohibited … Member States shall ensure that the video-sharing platform providers under their jurisdiction take appropriate measures to comply with the requirements set out in Article 9(1) with respect to audiovisual commercial communications that are not marketed, sold or arranged by those video-sharing platform providers" (English: "audiovisual commercial communications for medicinal products and medical treatment available only on prescription in the Member State within whose jurisdiction the media service provider falls shall be prohibited … Member States shall ensure that the video-sharing platform providers under their jurisdiction take appropriate measures to comply with the requirements set out in Article 9(1) with respect to audiovisual commercial communications that are not marketed, sold or arranged by those video-sharing platform providers")

claims.subject: advertising

claims.subject: controlled
claims.text: EU criminal drug-trafficking law defines 'drug' as substances covered by the UN 1961 and 1971 conventions plus the new psychoactive substances listed in its Annex; none of the course substances appears in that Annex (Framework Decision 2004/757/JHA, consolidated 12 January 2026), so controlled status is set by national and UN schedules.

claims.subject: compounding
